name: field
title: Field
description: The label, helper text, message and validation state around a form control.

base.summary: A column. The gap is the only measurement here, and it is deliberately tighter than it looks it should be.

tokens.gap: space.stack.2xs — not space.stack.xs: the label and the helper text each carry their own line-height leading, so the perceived gap is already larger than the number, and the next step up reads as separation rather than as grouping

label.summary: The control's name, at the label role of the type scale.

required-marker.summary: The asterisk. Required-ness is information, not a fault, so it is not the danger tone.

description.summary: Persistent helper text, and always ahead of the message in the description order so a constraint is heard before a failure.

message.summary: The status-dependent line. Neutral until the status says otherwise, so a field that has not been judged does not look judged.

tokens.when invalid: theme.danger-role.fg — the role's text colour on the page background, never its saturated bg, which is a non-text indicator tone

disabled.summary: Dimmed as a whole rather than removed, because the control underneath stays focusable and readable.

tokens.opacity: state.disabled-opacity, on the root so the label and helper text dim with the control

behavior.summary: Owns everything around a form control — the label, the required marker, the helper text, the message, and the `data-status` the control's own CSS selects on. Built on `getFieldProps`, which derives every id from the field's own and is the same primitive `TextField` has always used.

decisions.decision: The control arrives as a function, not as children
decisions.why: Field has to hand the control its `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `readOnly`. Of the three ways to do that, cloning `children` breaks the moment someone wraps their input in a fragment or a div; a context the control opts into makes a control rendered OUTSIDE a Field silently unlabelled, which is the failure this component exists to prevent. A function makes the wiring visible at the call site, works for a control from another library, and cannot be forgotten — there is nothing to render without it.

decisions.decision: It does not style the control's box
decisions.why: Height, inline padding, border and focus ring stay with each control, because they genuinely differ: a textarea grows with its content, a select reserves a well for its chevron, a checkbox is square and small. Field owning them would mean every control overriding them. What Field owns is what is identical across all of them — which is everything outside the box.

decisions.decision: `status` lives here rather than on the control
decisions.why: It drives `data-status` on the root, and each control's stylesheet selects on that for its own ring. One state, read by many controls, set in one place — and it is also what decides whether the message joins the description chain, which is an accessibility fact about the group rather than about the input.

decisions.decision: `TextField` keeps its flat API and is rebuilt on this, not replaced by it
decisions.why: `<TextField label="Email" />` stays one element with one prop — a component whose commonest use got more verbose to serve an abstraction would be a bad trade. Field is what TextField is made of. Callers reach for Field directly for the controls that have no wrapper yet and for third-party ones; everything else keeps the shorthand.

decisions.decision: The primitive is renamed `getFieldProps`, with the old name kept as an alias
decisions.why: It was called `getTextFieldProps`, and nothing in it has ever been about text: it returns `root`, `label`, `input`, `description` and `message` bags containing ids and ARIA, and a `<select>` or `<textarea>` could consume it unchanged today. A Select built on something called `getTextFieldProps` would be the lookup surface lying about itself. `getTextFieldProps` and `TextFieldStatus` continue to be exported as aliases so nothing outside this repo breaks.

decisions.decision: `disabled` is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native attribute
decisions.why: This system's rule, and for an input `readOnly` is the analogue of the button's click guard: it blocks editing while keeping the control in the tab order and the accessibility tree. Note the consequence, which is the same one `TextField`'s contract already carries — a readOnly field still submits its value.

decisions.decision: `labelHidden` hides the pixels, never the label
decisions.why: The label element is still rendered and still bound by `for`, so nothing about the accessible name changes. The alternative people reach for — dropping the label and letting `placeholder` stand in — loses the name on the first keystroke, which is when the reader most needs it.

use: A short noun phrase: "Billing email", not "Enter your billing email".
dont: Leaving it out for a field whose purpose looks obvious. There is no unlabelled option — `labelHidden` is how a visually bare field is built.
label.a11y: Bound to the control with `for`/`id` by the primitive, so it is the accessible name and clicking it focuses the control.

children.summary: Renders the control, given the id and ARIA it must carry.
use: Spreading the argument onto the control and nothing else: `{(control) => <select {...control} />}`.
Wrapping a control this system does not own yet, which is the case Field exists for outside its own components.
dont: Dropping the argument. A control rendered without it has no id, no accessible name and no description chain — and it will look correct, which is what makes it worth saying.
children.a11y: The argument carries `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `readOnly`. Every one of them is derived, so none can drift from the label and message beside it.

labelHidden.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A field whose meaning is already carried by its surroundings — a search box under a heading that names it.
dont: Using it and then relying on `placeholder` to carry the name. The placeholder disappears on the first keystroke.
labelHidden.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound. Nothing about the accessible name changes — only the pixels.

id.summary: Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an external error summary linking to the field it describes.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message — is derived from this, so a duplicate silently crosses two fields' wiring.

status.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the control's ring.
use: `validating` for an in-flight check, such as a uniqueness lookup.
`invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong and the colour says it twice; only the message says what.
status.a11y: `invalid` sets `aria-invalid` and pulls the message into `aria-describedby`; `validating` sets `aria-busy`. While `idle` the message stays on the page but leaves the description chain, so a stale message is not announced.

description.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: A constraint the reader needs before they type: a format, a limit, where the value ends up.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
description.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

message.summary: The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative: "Check this number."
dont: Putting the permanent constraint here. It vanishes from the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
message.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert: it is already in `aria-describedby`, and an assertive region would announce it a second time when focus lands.

required.summary: Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Fields that genuinely block submission. On a form where nearly everything is required, mark the optional ones instead.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. This renders one, and the second would be read out.
required.a11y: `aria-required` on the control. The rendered asterisk is `aria-hidden`, because announcing it too would say the requirement twice.

disabled.summary: Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.
use: A field whose value is decided elsewhere and should still be readable.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits — if the value must not reach the server, do not render the field.
disabled.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native attribute, so the field stays in the tab order and the accessibility tree.

className.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure or grid placement the form decides, which this component deliberately does not own.
dont: Restyling the label or message. Those come from the type scale, and a hand-written size drifts the moment the seed moves.

usage.case: A control this system does not wrap yet
usage.when: The case Field exists for: a native control with no component of its own.
usage.example:
<Field label="Country" description="Where the order ships.">
  {(control) => (
    <select {...control}>
      <option>Sri Lanka</option>
    </select>
  )}
</Field>
usage.notes: The argument is spread onto the control and nowhere else. Everything the reader hears — the name, the helper text, the requirement — is wired from it.

usage.when: Reporting what went wrong, where the reader can act on it.
usage.example:
<Field label="Card number" status="invalid" message="Check this number." required>
  {(control) => <input {...control} inputMode="numeric" />}
</Field>
usage.notes: The ring, the colour and the message say it three ways, and only the message says what to do. `status` also decides that the message joins the description chain — while idle it stays on the page and leaves the chain, so a stale error is not announced.

usage.case: A third-party control given the system's treatment
usage.when: A date picker or combobox from another library, which should still look and announce like every other field.
usage.notes: Field styles nothing inside the control, which is what makes this work — it owns the label, the helper text and the state, and leaves the box alone.

usage.when: The control already has a wrapper of its own.
usage.notes: Don't. `TextField` is built on Field and renders its own label, so this produces two labels and two ids for one input. `<TextField label="Email" />` is the whole thing — reach for Field only where no wrapper exists.
